breakdown.fullRead:
When there is more to do than hours in the day, what should you give up first? Most people pick sleep. It is quiet, nobody checks it, and the weekend seems ready to pay it back. Picture a full week. There is a deadline on Thursday, your child's school concert, a friend's party you offered to help plan and a stack of emails. Something has to give, and the night looks like the easiest place to find room.

That choice feels sensible, even grown-up. The hours in a day are fixed, and sleep looks like the only spare ones left. Some people wear a short night like a medal, proof of how hard they work. Others feel faintly ashamed of needing a full night, as if rest were for people who care less.

Greg McKeown says sleep should go last. He calls you the asset, the one tool that does all your important work. Wear that tool down, and everything it makes gets worse. A tired person still turns up to the meeting, still writes the report and still answers the child. They just do all of it worse.

His reason is about what sleep does for your mind. It keeps you able to think clearly, link ideas and choose what matters. That last skill sits at the centre of his whole approach, which is about doing less but better. The Nonessentialist, the person who tries to do everything, treats sleep as a luxury or even a sign of weakness. The Essentialist, the person who picks the few things that truly matter, treats it as a must. Without sleep, there is no sharp mind left to tell those few things from the noise.

McKeown points to a study of violin students by the researcher K. Anders Ericsson. The best players practiced the most, which is what you might expect. What surprises people is the rest of the finding. The best players also slept more than the others, and that included naps during the day. Their sleep did not steal from their practice. The players with the most serious practice behind them were also the best rested.

So the extra hour is not what it seems. Cutting sleep feels like finding time. But that hour belongs to a foggy mind, and a foggy mind makes worse choices about everything, including the work that matters most. It reads the same email three times. It says yes to things it would have turned down, because it can no longer tell what counts. A Saturday lie-in cannot go back and fix Wednesday's choices either. By then the week's real work is done, and a tired mind did it.

Every yes to one more task is a trade-off, meaning a choice that costs you something else. Stay up to fit a task in, and the cost comes out of your sleep, then out of tomorrow's work. Go back to that full week. The deadline matters, and so does your child's concert. The emails can wait a day, though, and the party plans can be handed to someone else. Moving one of those is a small loss. Two short nights would quietly damage everything else on the list. If you do not choose which task gives way, the week chooses for you, and it usually picks your sleep.

So when the week overflows, look at your list, not your pillow. When the hours run short, stop giving up sleep and give up a task instead, so a rested mind does what remains.

examples.title: Twelve prints and a midnight screen
examples.scenario: Zainab's camera club opens its yearly show on Saturday, and she still has twelve prints to edit. The prints will hang with her name under them. She also promised the club a slideshow for its website. It is 11:40 on Wednesday night, and her eyes sting from the screen. She could edit until two and sleep in on Sunday. Her cursor hovers over the next photo.
examples.whatToDo: Tell the club the slideshow comes next week, shut the laptop at your usual bedtime, and edit the prints rested.
examples.whyItMatters: Choosing the best shots takes a sharp eye, and that eye comes from sleep, not from two extra hours.

examples.title: An apprentice's Saturday lie-ins
examples.scenario: Callum is an apprentice joiner with a college test on Friday. For three weeks he has copied his notes into a neat new folder until one each morning. On weekends he sleeps till noon to catch up. His weekends have vanished, and on Wednesday he cut a door frame two centimetres short. He is still tired, and the test is two days away.
examples.whatToDo: Stop recopying the notes, study from the messy ones, and be in bed by eleven every weeknight, test week included.
examples.whyItMatters: Sleeping till noon on Sunday can't fix a tired Wednesday. Proper nights keep his measuring and his test answers sharp.

examples.title: The night before the nursery inspection
examples.scenario: Mireille leads the toddler room at a nursery, and inspectors arrive at eight tomorrow. It is nine at night. The wall display is half pinned, three children's progress notes are unfinished, and she planned a fresh parents' newsletter. Doing it all means working past two. Tomorrow she must answer hard questions while caring for twelve toddlers. Going to bed with the display half done makes her stomach turn.
examples.whatToDo: Finish the three progress notes, leave the display and the newsletter as they are, and be asleep by eleven.
examples.whyItMatters: Tomorrow the inspectors judge how she thinks and cares in the room, and that takes a rested head, not a new display.

questions.prompt: A garden centre owner has a big spring sale on Saturday. All week she sleeps four hours a night so she can finish every job on her list. What is the likely result?
choices: She clears the whole list, then sleeps it all off on Sunday.
She ticks off more boxes but makes worse calls about the sale itself.
She gets far more done, since every extra hour goes straight into the sale.
questions.explanation: Four-hour nights wear down the mind that has to run the sale, so the calls that count get worse. A Sunday lie-in comes after the sale, too late to help the week's work.

questions.prompt: A friend has three exams next week and works an evening shift at the cinema. They tell you, "I'll get by on five hours a night until it's over." What's your best reply?
choices: Swap your cinema shift with someone, and keep your normal sleep all week.
Sleep late on Sunday, so you start the exam week fully rested.
Find out first how much sleep you really need, then decide on your plans.
questions.explanation: Giving up the shift frees real hours, so full nights keep the mind sharp for every exam. A late Sunday helps one day, and the exams run all week on short nights.

questions.prompt: A project manager has a product launch on Thursday. Instead of working late, she drops the weekly newsletter she writes and keeps her normal bedtime. The launch goes smoothly. Why did that work?
choices: The extra sleep put her in a good mood, so she stayed keen all week.
Rested, she thought clearly about the launch, and the newsletter could wait a while.
The newsletter was her biggest job, so dropping it removed the most work.
questions.explanation: The launch needed good decisions, and a rested mind is what makes them. A good mood is pleasant, but her clear thinking, not her cheer, is what carried the launch.

questions.prompt: It's Sunday night. This week you lead a big client call on Wednesday, finish a report, and help your sister paint her flat two evenings. Fitting it all in means three late nights. What do you do?
choices: Move the client call to next week, to give yourself more prep time.
Ask your sister to move the painting, and keep your usual bedtime.
Work through lunch each day, so the late nights run shorter.
questions.explanation: Moving the painting frees two evenings, so you keep your sleep and bring a clear head to the call and the report. Moving the call drops the very work that needs your best mind.

questions.prompt: A food truck owner has a three-day festival and has also offered to cater a friend's party on Friday night. She plans to sleep five hours a night and lie in all Tuesday. What is the trap in her plan?
choices: Taking on all three festival days, which is a lot for one small truck.
Planning a lazy Tuesday, when she could use that day to restock.
Keeping the party and paying for it with the sleep the festival needs.
questions.explanation: The party is the extra job, and her short nights pay for it, so the festival gets a tired mind. Cutting festival days would drop her main work, the very thing her rest is for.

questions.prompt: Two architects split a bid due Friday. One drops a file clean-up she had planned and keeps her usual bedtime. The other stays up past two for three nights to polish his half. How do their two halves most likely compare?
choices: Her half comes out sharper, since she made each call with a rested head.
His half comes out stronger, since three extra nights of work went straight into it.
The halves come out about equal, since both start with the same skills.
questions.explanation: Her rested mind makes better calls on the bid, which is what wins it. His extra nights add hours, but a tired mind works them, so they buy less than they seem.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "The new work rota is due Friday, my son's science project is due too, and I chair the allotment committee. I'll cut my sleep and live on coffee." What do you say back?
choices: Switch to stronger coffee after lunch, so the short nights hurt less.
Keep your sleep, and rush through each job so all three still get done.
Step back from the committee this month, so your nights stay for sleep.
questions.explanation: Stepping back from the committee frees evenings, so sleep stays and a clear head handles the rota and the project. Stronger coffee hides the tiredness, but the tired mind still does the work.

reviewCards.front: Staying up late feels like gaining an hour, but that hour is ...
reviewCards.back: ... worked by a foggy mind that makes worse choices, so it buys much less than it seems.

reviewCards.front: A volunteer stayed up till two every night for a week planning a charity run. She kept every task on her list, and on race day sent the runners the wrong way. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: She cut sleep to keep every task. Dropping one smaller job would have left her a rested mind for the calls on race day.

reviewCards.front: In your own words: when your week has too much in it, what should go first, and why?
reviewCards.back: A task should go, not sleep, because a rested mind is the tool that does all your important work well.

reviewCards.front: It's 11 at night. You present to a new client at nine tomorrow. The ironing pile and a friend's birthday card are still waiting.
reviewCards.back: Leave the ironing for another day and write a short card in the morning. Go to bed now, so a rested mind runs the meeting.

reviewCards.front: Why can't a long lie-in on Sunday make up for a week of late nights?
reviewCards.back: Because the week's choices were already made by a tired mind. Sleep on Sunday can't go back and improve them.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Guarding your night's rest by trimming the to-do list whenever the week overflows.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down in the evening to finish work I didn't get to, I cross one smaller task off the list and still stop at my usual bedtime.
When I catch myself thinking I'll make up the sleep at the weekend, I pick one task this week that can wait, and move it off my list today.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before you go to bed tonight, look at tomorrow's list, move one smaller job to next week, and turn off the lights at your usual time.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each night this week, when work starts to run past your bedtime, drop one smaller task instead of the sleep. On Sunday, look back at the tasks you dropped and how your mornings felt.

chapters.title: When Pretty Good Should Mean No
chapters.hook: Your week is a suitcase stuffed with things you rated a seven. Now the one thing you'd call a ten won't fit.
chapters.counterintuition: You have probably been told that a pretty good offer, say a 70 out of 100, is worth a yes. The trouble is that pretty good options are everywhere and fill every hour, so only a 90 or above should get in.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Score each option on the one thing that matters most, and treat anything under 90 as a no.
chapters.tryThisNow: Score one thing you've agreed to this week before lunch today, 0 to 100 on what matters most, and drop it if it's under 90.

memorableLines.text: Pretty good fills the week. Only a 90 or better earns your yes.

breakdown.fastRead:
A pretty good offer is usually one to turn down. Every 70 you accept takes room a 95 would need. Greg McKeown's test for this is the 90 percent rule. Score an option from 0 to 100 on the one thing that matters most. Anything under 90 counts as a 0 and gets a no. Derek Sivers, who started the online music store CD Baby, lives by a similar rule. If he does not feel a strong, clear yes, he says no.

Saying yes to a 70 feels sensible, since turning down something good feels wasteful. But good options are everywhere. A loose test lets nearly all of them in, and you end up stuck with the merely good and no room for the best. McKeown's fix is extreme criteria, a bar so high that only the top few things clear it.

A coworker invites you onto a new planning group. First, name the one test that matters most, such as whether it moves your main project forward. It would help that project a little, so you score it a 70. A score under 90 becomes a 0, so you say no. Your Thursday afternoon stays free for work you would score a 95. People who count every score under 90 as a no keep their time for the few things they would call great.

breakdown.fullRead:
A pretty good offer is usually one to turn down. Every 70 you accept takes room a 95 would need. That sounds wrong at first. A 70 is a solid score, well above half, and most of life asks you to settle for less. Yet a week packed with 70s has no space left when something truly great comes along.

Greg McKeown gives a simple tool for this, which he calls the 90 percent rule. Pick the single most important test for a choice. Score the option from 0 to 100 against that test. If it scores below 90, change the score to 0 and drop it. The sharp cut stops you getting stuck in the middle. A 70 never gets to sit around as a maybe, waiting for a free hour.

Derek Sivers, who started the online music store CD Baby, lives by a similar rule. If he does not feel a strong, clear yes about something, he says no to it. A shrug is a no. A mild yes is a no too. Only an eager yes gets through, however good the offer looks on paper.

Most people work the other way, and for good reasons. Turning down something good feels wasteful, even rude. A 70 could lead somewhere, and saying no might close a door. So people use a loose test, such as whether a thing could be useful. The trouble is that good options are everywhere. A loose test lets nearly all of them in, and you end up stuck with the merely good and no room for the best.

McKeown sets two kinds of people side by side. The Nonessentialist, someone who says yes to nearly everything, takes most requests that seem fine. The Essentialist, someone who does less but better, keeps yes for only the top slice of options. The gap between them comes down to trade-offs, meaning every yes to one thing is a no to something else. Your hours are limited. If you do not choose what fills them, other people's requests will choose for you.

That is why McKeown argues for extreme criteria, a bar so high that only the top few things clear it. A loose test asks whether something is good. A high bar asks whether it is the best. The first question gets a yes almost every time. The second gets a yes only rarely, and that rare yes gets your full effort.

Using the rule takes three steps. First, name the one thing that matters most for this choice. Next, score the offer from 0 to 100 on that one thing, and be honest rather than hopeful. Then make the cut. Anything from 90 up is a yes. Anything below 90 is a no, even an 89.

A coworker invites you onto a new planning group. Your one test is whether it moves your main project forward. It would help that project a little, so you score it a 70. A score under 90 becomes a 0, so you say no. Your Thursday afternoon stays free for work you would score a 95. People who count every score under 90 as a no keep their time for the few things they would call great.

examples.title: Twenty small accounts on offer
examples.scenario: Carmen sells office furniture, and her goal this quarter is to grow her sales as much as she can. A deal with the city university would do that, and it needs her full attention. At Monday's sales meeting, her manager offers her twenty small shop accounts. On sales growth, she scores them a 70. Her manager waits, pen over the sign-up sheet.
examples.whatToDo: Count the 70 as a 0, turn down the small accounts, and keep her days for the university deal.
examples.whyItMatters: Twenty decent accounts would eat the calls and hours the university deal needs, and that deal is her 95.

examples.title: A folder of twelve songs
examples.scenario: Rohan has guitar lessons every Saturday, and he wants one song ready for an open-mic night in March. His teacher gave him a list to choose from. He liked most of them, so he kept every song he rated a seven or better. Now twelve sit in his folder. With three weeks left, he can't play one cleanly, and his teacher sighs.
examples.whatToDo: Score each song on one thing, how well he can play it by March, and drop every song under 90.
examples.whyItMatters: Twelve half-learned songs leave him nothing to play, while one that scores high gives him a song he owns.

examples.title: Her brother's hot sauce stall
examples.scenario: Priyanka's older brother is starting a Saturday market stall for his hot sauce, and he wants her beside him every week. On her one goal this year, passing her nursing exams, she scores it a 70. Saturdays are her study days. When she hesitates, he says, "You're the only one I trust with this." She dreads seeing his face fall.
examples.whatToDo: Count the 70 as a 0, and tell him warmly that her Saturdays belong to her exams until they're done.
examples.whyItMatters: A yes out of fear would cost her the study days her exams need, and he'd get a half-present partner.

questions.prompt: Your friend's main goal this year is finishing her first novel. A local writers' group invites her to meet every Saturday morning. She says, "For the novel, it's a solid 70. Good enough for a yes, right?" What's your best reply?
choices: "Yes, a 70 is well above half, so join the group while you're asked."
"Rate it on fun, friends and cost too, then average them."
"A 70 for the novel is a no, so keep your Saturdays free."
questions.explanation: She scored the group on the novel and got a 70, which is under 90, so it's a no. Averaging in fun and friends would only pull a weak fit up into a yes.

questions.prompt: A bakery owner adds a new item only if it scores 90 or more on one question: will regulars come back for it? His menu stays short, and the few items sell out. Why does his approach work?
choices: Turning down the good items leaves room and effort for the best few.
A short menu looks more expert, so customers trust the bakery more.
Testing every item on what regulars want weeds out the ones that taste bad.
questions.explanation: Every pretty good item would take oven space and baking time. Saying no to them leaves room for the few he's sure of. A 70 item tastes fine and still crowds out the best.

questions.prompt: A former coworker messages to invite you to co-host her weekly podcast. It sounds fun, and you feel a rush of excitement. Your top goal this year is making your dog-walking business pay all your bills. What do you do first?
choices: Say yes while the excitement is still fresh, and sort out the details later.
Tell her you'll think it over, and leave the invite open.
Score the podcast on how much it helps the business, before replying.
questions.explanation: Excitement isn't the test; your business is. Score the podcast on how much it helps, and you'll know if it reaches 90. Leaving the invite open decides nothing and keeps it hanging over your week.

questions.prompt: Your cousin wants a job in data work, and that is his one test for a weekend course. A coding course scores an 85. He says, "That's so close to 90 it basically counts." Where is the trap in his thinking?
choices: Thinking one test is too narrow for a choice this big.
Thinking a score just under the bar is close enough to count.
Thinking he can decide this without first asking someone who works in data.
questions.explanation: An 85 is under 90, so it counts as a 0. Rounding up is how pretty good options slip in. Asking someone in data work wouldn't change that, since his own score is already in.

questions.prompt: A retired teacher volunteers mainly to tutor adults learning to read. She also says yes to every group whose request seems pretty good: a book sale, a park clean-up, a food drive. What is likely after a few months?
choices: The tutoring she cares about most gets only the scraps of her time.
She gets better at juggling, so each group gets a fair share.
The groups see her effort and start offering her the roles she wants most.
questions.explanation: Good requests keep coming, and each yes takes hours. Before long the tutoring, her main reason for volunteering, gets squeezed. Juggling faster can't keep up when nearly every request gets in.

questions.prompt: A coworker has turned down every offer scoring under 90 on her goal of becoming a manager. Now the director offers to mentor her, and she scores it a 95. She says, "I've said no to so much lately. Maybe this should go too." What should you tell her?
choices: "Turn it down too, since doing less means saying no almost every time."
"A 95 is the kind of offer all those no's were for."
"Score it again next week, in case the 95 was excitement."
questions.explanation: All those no's made room for an offer like this. A 95 on her main goal clears 90, so it's a yes. Rescoring next week just lets a top offer drift while she doubts it.

questions.prompt: A couple house hunting agrees on one test: a short walk to their kids' school. Any home scoring under 90 on it is out, however nice the kitchen. They stop losing weekends to viewings. What makes this approach work?
choices: Homes that are only fairly close get a clear no, not a maybe.
A nice kitchen matters less to most families than a short walk to school.
Fewer viewings leave them more free weekends to rest and plan.
questions.explanation: The sharp cut turns every so-so home into a no on the spot, so nothing lingers as a maybe. Kitchen versus school walk is just their choice of test, not what makes the method work.

reviewCards.front: A man said yes to a darts league, coaching his niece's netball team and a side job, each a decent 7 out of 10. By spring he had no evenings left for the woodworking he loves most. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He let every pretty good offer in. Scoring each one on his woodworking time and counting anything under 90 as a no would have kept his evenings free.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, how do you decide which offers earn a yes?
reviewCards.back: Pick the one thing that matters most, score the offer from 0 to 100 on it, and say no to anything under 90.

reviewCards.front: A neighbor asks you to help run a weekly kids' cooking club. On your top goal this year, getting fit for a long hike, you'd score it a 75. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Count the 75 as a 0 and say no kindly. A decent fit would still take the evenings your training needs.

reviewCards.front: Why can a string of pretty good yeses hurt more than a clear no?
reviewCards.back: Good options are everywhere, and each yes takes room. Soon there's none left for the few things that are truly the best.

reviewCards.front: An option scores 85 on the thing that matters most to you. It counts as ...
reviewCards.back: ... a 0, so it's a no, and the time stays free for something that scores 90 or more.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Judging each choice by a single top test and turning away anything short of near-perfect.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down to my messages at the start of the workday, I score each new request 0 to 100 on my main goal and turn down anything under 90.
When I catch myself agreeing to something that's only pretty good, I score it on what matters most and, if it's under 90, take the yes back that same day.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before bed tonight, write down the one thing that matters most to you this month. Score your next three plans against it, and cancel any that come in under 90.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Sunday evening, list what you've agreed to for the week ahead. Score each item on your one top goal, and drop or turn down anything under 90.

chapters.title: One Aim Worth Chasing, Clear Enough to Check
chapters.hook: Hang a warm motto on the wall, and your team keeps arguing. Give them one clear aim worth chasing, and the arguing fades.
chapters.counterintuition: A fine mission statement or a goals list keeps everyone on track. It sounds right, and it fails for one reason: nobody steers by words too vague to test or goals too small to care about. Set one aim people care about and can check.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Set one aim that is exciting enough to care about and clear enough to know when it's met.
chapters.tryThisNow: Put one object that stands for your main aim this season, like walking boots or a guitar, beside your front door tonight.

memorableLines.text: One aim people care about and can check settles a thousand small fights.

breakdown.fastRead:
The volunteers at Teodora's animal shelter can't agree on anything. So she chalks a motto on the board by the door: Every animal deserves love. By noon the dog walkers want a bigger yard, the cat team a new room, and the fundraisers a fancy dinner. Each group says the motto backs them. Two volunteers have already quit, and she can't lose more.

A warm motto can't choose between good plans, so people fight for their own plans. A list of small targets is clear, but nobody cares much. Greg McKeown's answer is an essential intent, one aim that is both inspiring and clear enough to check. Made once, it answers a thousand later questions. Martha Lane Fox took on the job of getting more people in the UK using the internet. She set one plain aim: get people across the country online. That aim guided her later choices.

Test any aim with two questions: would people care, and would you know the day it was met? Teodora wipes the board and writes: Every animal here finds a home within a month. Now the yard, the room and the dinner face one question: which gets animals home faster? When your group pulls different ways, give it one aim worth caring about and plain enough to check, and small choices settle themselves.

breakdown.fullRead:
The volunteers at Teodora's animal shelter can't agree on anything. So she chalks a motto on the board by the door: Every animal deserves love. Everyone nods, and for an hour it feels like a fresh start. By noon the dog walkers want a bigger yard, the cat team a new room, and the fundraisers a fancy dinner. Each group points at the motto and says it backs them. Two volunteers have already quit, and she can't lose more.

Her move seemed sensible, since a warm motto is easy to agree with. That is exactly the trouble. A line everyone agrees with can't choose between two good plans, so it settles nothing. Greg McKeown says that when people aren't sure what their group is aiming at, two things tend to happen. Some turn to politics and spend their energy winning the leader's attention. Others quietly chase their own plans, and the group's effort scatters. Both look like hard work, yet neither moves the shelter forward.

The usual fix is to swap the motto for a list of targets for the next few months. Raise a set sum by spring. Walk every dog twice a day. Post three photos a week. Each target is clear and easy to tick off. McKeown points to the catch: goals like these are too small for anyone to care about. So a leader often ends up with one kind of goal that inspires but can't guide, and another that guides but can't inspire.

His answer is an essential intent. That is one aim that is both inspiring and clear enough to check, meaningful and measurable at once. He sees it as one decision that makes a thousand others. Settle it carefully once, and each new idea can be held up against it. Nobody has to wait for the leader to rule on every request, because the aim does the ruling.

Martha Lane Fox took on the job of getting more people in the UK using the internet. She set one plain aim: get people across the country online. It was easy to care about and easy to check against. That aim then guided her later choices.

You can test any aim with two questions. Would the people involved care about it? Would you know the day it was met? A motto passes the first test and fails the second. A target list passes the second and fails the first. To fix a motto, add the check: what will be true, and by when? To fix a target, tie it to something people care about. The same tests work for a team at work, a group of friends or a family planning its summer.

Teodora wipes the board and writes: Every animal here finds a home within a month. The volunteers can feel that aim, because they came for the animals. They can check it too, one animal at a time. Now the yard, the room and the dinner face one question: which gets animals home faster? The volunteers can answer that without her. When your group pulls different ways, give it one aim worth caring about and plain enough to check, and small choices settle themselves.

examples.title: The yearly promise to get fit together
examples.scenario: Last spring, Sione and four friends promised over a barbecue to get fit together. One bought a gym pass, one tried yoga twice, and the rest did nothing. Now they are back at the same grill in the same garden, burgers spitting. Someone says, "We should really get fit this year." Everyone nods, exactly like last time.
examples.whatToDo: Offer one aim the whole group would enjoy and could check: all five of you on top of the big hill outside town by July.
examples.whyItMatters: A promise to get fit gives nobody a reason to move on a Tuesday. A shared hilltop date tells each friend what this week's walk is for.

examples.title: Twelve goals taped beside the till
examples.scenario: Yusuf runs a busy noodle bar. In January he taped twelve goals for the quarter beside the till: cut food waste, post online twice a week, try a new soup, and nine more. His staff ticked off the easy ones. Meanwhile the lunch queue still snakes out the door, and regulars have started eating at the place across the street.
examples.whatToDo: Take down the list and give the staff one aim they care about and can count: every lunch bowl on the table within ten minutes of ordering.
examples.whyItMatters: The soup, the posts and the waste plan now face one test: do they get lunch out faster?

examples.title: Maths homework that ends in shouting
examples.scenario: Every evening Astrid sits with her daughter Elif at the coffee table to help with maths homework. Astrid's aim is simple: get your grades up. Elif, who spends her weekends building little robots, shoves the worksheet away. "That's your goal, not mine," she says. Most nights end with both of them dreading the next one.
examples.whatToDo: Ask Elif what she'd be proud of, then shape it together into one aim she can check, like the maths grade the school robotics club asks for.
examples.whyItMatters: An aim Elif cares about turns each worksheet into a step toward robots, not a fight about who's in charge.

questions.prompt: A family running two holiday cottages agrees on one aim for the summer: every guest leaves a five-star review. That same evening they settle new towels, the welcome basket and the website. Why did those choices come so easily?
choices: Each choice could be tested against a result they all cared about.
They had agreed to stop arguing and trust each other's taste for once.
Reviews are easy to count, so the small tasks looked simple.
questions.explanation: Every option faced one test: will this help each guest leave five stars? The family cared about that result, and it was easy to check. Easy counting alone would not have settled the towels.

questions.prompt: You coach a kids' volleyball team. Your goal for the season, printed on the sign-up sheet, is to have fun and grow as players. Parents keep asking why practice runs the way it does. What do you do?
choices: Keep the goal for now, and pick a clearer one when the season ends.
Choose one aim you can check, like every child serving overhand by spring.
Set five targets for the season, such as wins and points scored.
questions.explanation: Fun and growth can't explain any one choice about practice. Every child serving overhand by spring is something families care about and anyone can check. Win and point targets are clear but too small to rally anyone.

questions.prompt: A hostel manager tells staff the aim this quarter is to cut laundry costs by eight percent. Staff hit the number. The rooms look shabbier, and two cleaners hand in their notice. What was the trap?
choices: The target was set far too low, so staff relaxed once they hit it.
Staff could measure the aim, but it gave them nothing to care about.
The manager said the target out loud instead of writing it down.
questions.explanation: Cutting laundry costs was easy to check, but nobody felt it was worth their best work. Writing the number down would still have left a small aim nobody cared about.

questions.prompt: A new manager at a call centre gives her team a motto, "We put customers first," and no other aim. Three supervisors each want a different change to how calls are handled. What is likely to happen next?
choices: Staff feel inspired by the motto and work harder on every call.
The supervisors pick whichever change most callers asked for, then move on quickly.
Each supervisor lobbies the manager for their own change, and little else moves.
questions.explanation: A motto everyone agrees with can't pick between three plans, so each supervisor fights for their own and tries to win the manager over. Feeling inspired doesn't help when nobody can tell which change comes first.

questions.prompt: A friend who sells handmade candles online tells you, "This year my goal is just to grow the business." What is the most helpful thing to say back?
choices: What growth would excite you, and how will you know you got there?
Try lots of new scents this year and keep whichever ones sell.
That's a good goal, so start by fixing the website and the product photos.
questions.explanation: Growing the business is too vague to guide any choice. Asking what growth would excite your friend, and how they'd know, turns it into a real aim. Trying lots of scents leaves no way to judge which ones matter.

questions.prompt: A six-person app team used to argue over every new feature. Then they agreed on one aim: any grandparent can start a video call within a minute of opening the app. Since then, debates take minutes. Why did they shrink?
choices: Everyone wanted that result, and each new feature could be tested against it.
The strict one-minute limit made people too nervous to suggest extra features.
Building only for grandparents is a narrow job, so there was less to build.
questions.explanation: Every feature now faces one question the whole team cares about and can test: does it get a grandparent calling within a minute? A smaller job alone would still leave plenty to argue over.

questions.prompt: You and two flatmates have money to spend on the shared living room. One wants a sofa, one wants a big TV, and one wants a dining table. What should come first?
choices: Vote on each item one by one until the money runs out.
Price every item, then drop the dearest ones until the total fits the budget.
Agree on one shared aim, like having friends over for dinner every Sunday.
questions.explanation: Dinner with friends every Sunday is something all three can care about and check, and it quickly ranks the table, sofa and TV. Voting item by item just leaves three people pushing their own pick.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what kind of aim stops a group from pulling in different directions?
reviewCards.back: One aim the people involved truly care about, plain enough that you'd know the day it's met. It settles the small choices for you.

reviewCards.front: You and a friend run a podcast together, and every week you argue about guests, topics and when to record.
reviewCards.back: Agree on one aim you both care about and can check, like a new episode every Friday until summer. Then judge each guest and topic by it.

reviewCards.front: Why does a warm motto like 'We care about people' often leave a team still arguing?
reviewCards.back: It's too vague to choose between good plans, so everyone says it backs their own idea, and nothing gets settled.

reviewCards.front: An aim is ready to guide your choices when people care about it and ...
reviewCards.back: ... you could tell, on a set day, whether it has been met.

reviewCards.front: A manager told the team their aim was to be the best team in the company. Six months later nobody could say if they'd made it, and the old fights were back. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The aim inspired people but gave them no way to check it. Saying what would be true, and by when, would have let it settle the fights.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Turning a fuzzy hope into one target that people want to reach and can check off.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself thinking, we should really get better at this, I name one result I'd be proud of and the day I'd check it.
When I sit down to plan the coming week with my team or family, I ask which one result we'd all be glad to reach, and how we'd know.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the day ends, say one aim out loud to someone in a group you belong to. Make it one they'd care about and you could check by a set date, then ask if it lands.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, when your team or household faces a choice between two good plans, ask which one brings your shared aim closer, and let that answer decide.

chapters.title: A Clear No That Keeps the Friendship Warm
chapters.hook: A good friend is asking for your Sunday. You need to say no, and you can already feel the friendship cooling.
chapters.counterintuition: The usual advice is to say yes when someone you care about asks, since a no sounds like you don't care. Saying no to the request while showing warmth to the person works better, because the decision and the friendship are two separate things.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When you turn someone down, refuse the request, not the person, and tell them warmly that they still matter.
chapters.tryThisNow: Answer one request you've left hanging today, giving a clear no and one warm, true sentence about the person who asked.

memorableLines.text: Say no to the favour and yes to the friend.

breakdown.fastRead:
Can you say no to someone you care about and leave them sure they still matter to you? Most people doubt it. So they say yes to things they don't want, or hide behind a vague maybe.

Greg McKeown says people freeze because they blend two things, the decision about the request and their feelings for the person. Pull them apart, and you can give a clear no with real warmth. You may lose a little goodwill in the moment, but people come to respect someone whose yes means something. McKeown shows this with Stephen R. Covey, the well-known leadership writer, who took his daughter Cynthia to San Francisco and promised her their time together. An old college friend asked him to dinner, and he kindly said no to keep his evening with her. Years later, Cynthia still remembered that night as proof of how much she mattered.

A no hurts a friendship only when it sounds like a no to the friend, and a dodge or a cold one-line text sounds just like that. So give the no plainly, and in the same breath name a real thing you value in the person. Turn down the request and tell them warmly that they still matter, and they will feel valued while you keep your time.

Turn down the request and tell them warmly that they still matter, and they will feel valued while you keep your time.

In the moment the two seem tied together, so turning down the favour feels like turning down the friend. Pull them apart, and the problem shrinks. He is blunt about why the no matters. Every yes is a trade-off, meaning it takes time and energy from something else you care about. If you can't say no, other people end up deciding how your days are spent. He also admits the price. A no can make you a little less popular in the moment. Over time, though, people come to respect someone whose yes means something.

McKeown tells a story from Cynthia Covey, daughter of the well-known leadership writer Stephen R. Covey. Her father took her on a trip to San Francisco and promised her their time together. While they were there, an old college friend asked him to dinner. Saying yes would have cost Cynthia her evening. He kindly said no and kept his time with her. Years later, she still remembered that night as proof of how much she mattered to him.

Look at who heard what. The friend heard a no to one dinner, and it came kindly, not as a brush-off. The daughter heard that she came first, and it stayed with her for years. The choice protected the evening. The kindness protected the friendship.

A no hurts a friendship only when it sounds like a no to the friend. Several common moves sound just like that. A vague maybe leaves the person waiting and guessing. A cold one-line text gives the decision with nothing for the person. A pile of nervous excuses turns the talk into a trial, as if the friend has to be won over. Even a heavy apology does harm, because it treats the no as a wound to them.

Here is the fix worked through once. An old friend asks you to read his three-hundred-page novel draft by the end of the month. You have a new baby, and the few quiet evenings you get belong to sleep. So you tell him plainly that you can't read the whole draft this month. In the same breath you name a real thing you value, like how much you loved the first story he ever showed you. If there is a small part you are glad to do, offer it, such as reading the opening chapter. You don't even need the word no to be clear. He loses a reader for the month, and he knows he hasn't lost you.

So the puzzle has an answer. Turn down the request and tell them warmly that they still matter, and they will feel valued while you keep your time.

examples.title: An old apprentice asks for a week
examples.scenario: Femi lays tiles for a living, and his phone rings as he wipes grout off a bathroom floor. It's Bruno, his old apprentice, who has just won his first big job on his own. Bruno wants Femi on site all next week. Femi's diary is already full of promised kitchens. He is proud of Bruno, and he grips the wet sponge, unsure what to say.
examples.whatToDo: Tell Bruno plainly that next week is full, then say how proud you are that he won this job on his own.
examples.whyItMatters: Bruno loses the extra hands but hears that his old boss believes in him, so the bond stays strong.

examples.title: Clean-up day, one year on
examples.scenario: This morning Gus from next door knocked to ask Annika to run the street clean-up day again. Last spring she said yes to keep things friendly, though she didn't want to. It ate three weekends. She snapped at Gus over a late delivery of bin bags, and since then the two of them barely wave across the hedge.
examples.whatToDo: Tell Gus kindly that you won't run it this year, and that you've missed your chats over the hedge.
examples.whyItMatters: Her forced yes hurt the friendship it was meant to save. A clear no with warmth can start to mend it.

examples.title: The Sunday practice partner
examples.scenario: Javier takes an evening sign language class, and his classmate Mei asked him to practise with her every Sunday morning. He said no, then added a quick 'you're great though' as he packed up his bag. Mei heard it as a polite brush-off. Tonight she sits on the far side of the room and doesn't look up when he waves.
examples.whatToDo: Tell Mei the Sundays are still a no, and name one real thing you value, like her patience with your finger spelling.
examples.whyItMatters: A rushed, general compliment sounds like an exit line. A specific one shows the no was about Sundays, not about her.

questions.prompt: Your cousin asks you to handle all the food for his engagement party next month. You know you can't take it on. What do you do?
choices: Tell him you'll think it over, and hope the question quietly fades before the party.
Tell him you can't do the food, and say how happy you are to celebrate with him.
List everything already on your plate this month, so he can see the no isn't about him.
questions.explanation: Saying no to the food while saying how happy you are for him keeps the job and the person apart. Hoping a maybe fades is a dodge, and a dodge sounds like a no to him.

questions.prompt: A woman turns down a friend's request to help paint his new flat. She apologises again and again and calls herself a terrible friend. Now he keeps comforting her. What trap did she fall into?
choices: Turning down the painting when she could have offered to help him for one hour.
Giving her answer in person rather than sending a short, kind message first.
Treating her no as a blow to him, not just to his painting plan.
questions.explanation: Her no was about the painting, but the heavy apology made it sound like a blow to him. A plain no with one warm, true line would have done. Offering an hour leaves that apology in place.

questions.prompt: A team lead turns down a coworker's invitation to join his new committee. She says plainly she can't take it on, then tells him his idea is strong and she's glad he's leading it. What most likely happens next?
choices: He's let down about the committee, but still comes to her for advice.
He takes it as a sign she doesn't value him, and quietly stops including her.
He reads the praise as a hint she'll join, and asks again.
questions.explanation: She turned down the committee, not him, and said so warmly. He loses her time on the project but keeps a colleague who values him. Her no was plain, so the praise gives him no reason to ask again.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My old teammate wants me to coach his kid's basketball team. Saying no feels mean, so I keep telling him maybe." What is your best reply?
choices: "Tell him plainly you can't coach, and say how much the old team meant to you."
"Say yes for one season, then step back quietly once he finds someone else."
"Ask him for a week to check your calendar, and give him your real answer after that."
questions.explanation: Your friend already wants to say no, and the maybe is only stalling. A plain no with a warm word about the old team shows the no is about coaching, not him. A week with the calendar just stalls longer.

questions.prompt: A pharmacist is asked by an old friend to join his pub quiz team every Thursday. She says she can't give up another evening, then tells him how much she loves their Sunday phone calls. They stay as close as ever. Why did this work?
choices: Her friend didn't care much about the quiz team in the first place.
She kept the no about the quiz nights and the warmth about her friend.
Her friend could tell how worn out she was, so he let it go easily.
questions.explanation: Her no was about Thursday nights, and her warm words were about him, so he lost a quiz partner, not a friend. Looking tired might explain a no, but it says nothing about whether she values him.

questions.prompt: A coworker asks you to cover his early shifts for the next two weeks. You say no and tell him you really like working alongside him. He sighs and says he's stuck. What is your move now?
choices: Keep your no, say you hope he finds cover soon, and stay friendly.
Give in and cover the shifts, since he sounds so stuck.
Explain to him again, in more detail, why your early mornings are already full.
questions.explanation: The no was clear and the warmth was real. Keeping both steady tells him the answer stands and he still matters. Giving in now would spend two weeks of your mornings and empty out the no you gave.

questions.prompt: A man's sister asks him to help on her yoga studio's opening day. He texts back, "Can't, sorry." A week later he sends flowers to make up for it, but she is still cool with him. What did he get wrong?
choices: Answering his sister by text rather than calling her to explain himself.
Sending flowers, a gesture too small to make up for such a big no.
Hoping warmth sent a week later could mend a no that came cold.
questions.explanation: His no came with nothing warm, so it sounded like a no to her. Flowers a week later arrived after that feeling had set in. A text would have been fine with one warm line in it.

reviewCards.front: A friend asks you to help sew costumes for her children's theatre group this month, and you've decided you can't.
reviewCards.back: Tell her plainly you can't do the sewing, and in the same breath name something real you admire about her or the group.

reviewCards.front: Why does a clear no often hurt a friendship less than a long run of maybes?
reviewCards.back: A maybe blurs the request with the person and leaves them guessing. A clear no with warmth shows you're turning down the task and still value them.

reviewCards.front: When you say no to someone you care about, the warm part goes ...
reviewCards.back: ... in the same message as the no, so they hear both at once and never wonder whether the no was about them.

reviewCards.front: Someone turned down a colleague's project with a one-line email, then wondered why the colleague went quiet for weeks.
reviewCards.back: The no came with nothing warm, so it read like a verdict on the colleague. One true, kind sentence about them, sent with the no, would have kept the two apart.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, how do you say no without pushing someone away?
reviewCards.back: Say no to what they ask, then tell them warmly and truthfully what they mean to you, so the no stays about the request.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Keeping a refusal about the task while showing the person, out loud, that you still value them.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I hear myself say maybe just to dodge saying no, I go back to the person that same day with a clear no and one warm, true line about them.
When I open my messages at the start of the workday, I answer each request I'm turning down with a plain no and one true thing I value about the sender.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the day ends, think of one person likely to ask you for something soon. Write down one true thing you value about them, so it's ready if a no is needed.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of each week, look back at the requests you turned down. For each one, check whether the person heard something warm and true with the no, and note which went out cold so your next no carries the warm line.

chapters.title: Stop Paying More to Rescue Money Already Gone
chapters.hook: Walking away from a failing plan wastes nothing. The money and months already in it are gone whether you stay or go.
chapters.counterintuition: We tend to keep paying into a project that isn't working, so what we've already spent won't be wasted. What works is judging it only by what it will cost from here, since nothing we do now can bring the past spending back.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When something is failing, ignore what you have already spent and judge only what it costs from here.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write one line today naming a failing plan and what it will cost you from here, then tape it to your fridge door.

memorableLines.text: Spent is spent. Decide by what staying will cost you from today.

breakdown.fastRead:
The worst reason to keep going is how much you have already put in. Greg McKeown shows this with the Concorde, a passenger jet that flew faster than sound. The British and French governments kept paying for it for years. They kept paying long after it was clear the plane would never earn back what it cost.

He calls this sunk-cost bias, the pull to keep putting time or money into something because of what has already gone in. It feels sensible, since quitting seems to turn all that spending into waste. But the money already spent is gone whether you stay or walk away. Only what you spend from now on can still be saved.

So when a plan is failing, leave the past out and ask one question. If you weren't already in it, would you sign up today for what it will cost from here? Say you are 300 pages into a thick novel you dislike, with 400 still to go. Would you buy it today for those evenings? If not, admit it was a bad pick and close it, and the evenings are yours again. Once you judge a failing plan only by what it costs from here, your time and money stop chasing what is already gone.

The worst reason to keep going is how much you have already put in. Greg McKeown shows this with the Concorde, a passenger jet that flew faster than sound. The British and French governments kept paying for it for years. They kept paying long after it was clear the plane would never earn back what it cost. He calls this sunk-cost bias, the pull to keep putting time or money into something because of what has already gone in. It feels sensible, and that is why it is so common. Quitting seems to turn all that spending into waste, as if walking away were the moment the loss happens. It isn't. The money already spent is gone whether you stay or walk away. Only what you spend from now on can still be saved.

A second pull makes this worse. He calls it the endowment effect, which means valuing a thing more simply because it is yours. A plan you started or a project with your name on it looks better to you than it would if a stranger offered it. Together, the two pulls can keep you inside a commitment long after it stopped serving you.

The first step is to pretend you don't own it yet. Ask what you would give to get it now, as if it were on offer for the first time. If you weren't already in, would you sign up today for what it will cost from here? That question leaves the past out of the sum, which is where it belongs.

Next, admit the mistake. Saying plainly that you got something wrong can feel like losing, but it ends the need to defend the past. Then face the fear of wasting. Stopping feels wasteful because you can see what went in. The real waste is the next month poured into the same hole.

Watch the small, offhand promises too, like saying you could probably help with something while passing in a corridor. They quietly turn into commitments you feel you own, and the same pulls keep you in them. He suggests stopping for a moment before you offer, so the offhand yes never gets made.

When you can't tell whether something is still worth it, he suggests a reverse pilot. A normal pilot tests something new on a small scale. A reverse pilot quietly stops something to see whether anyone notices. If you stop writing a long weekly summary and nobody asks where it went, you have your answer, and finding out cost almost nothing.

Say you are 300 pages into a thick novel you dislike, with 400 still to go. Would you buy it today for those evenings? If not, call it a bad pick and close it, and the evenings are yours again. Once you judge a failing plan only by what it costs from here, your time and money stop chasing what is already gone.

examples.title: The washing machine that keeps breaking
examples.scenario: Emeka has paid for three repairs on his old washing machine this year. Tonight it stopped mid-cycle again, with his work shirts still dripping in the drum. The repairman quotes another fix at almost half the price of a new machine. Emeka keeps thinking of everything he has already spent keeping it going. His thumb hovers over the repairman's number.
examples.whatToDo: Leave the three old bills out of it. Compare only this repair with a new machine, and choose whichever costs less from here.
examples.whyItMatters: Those old bills are gone either way, so they can't make a fourth repair on a failing machine the cheaper choice.

examples.title: A module dragging down the degree
examples.scenario: Freya added an optional statistics module to her history degree and fell behind by week four. Not wanting to waste a month of work, she paid for weekend tutoring and gave up two bookshop shifts. Her statistics mark is still failing, and her last history essay came back a grade lower. The deadline to drop is Friday, and she feels sick at the thought of quitting.
examples.whatToDo: Ask whether she'd pick the module today, knowing what the rest of term will take, and drop it by Friday if not.
examples.whyItMatters: The tutoring and the lost shifts can't be won back, but dropping now protects her history marks and her pay.

examples.title: Five minutes before the clinic opens
examples.scenario: Dariusz runs the front desk at a walk-in clinic. He has spent forty minutes setting up a new check-in tablet, and it still freezes on the first screen. The doors open in five minutes, and patients are already lining up outside in the rain. A box of paper sign-in forms sits under the counter. "Just one more restart," he mutters.
examples.whatToDo: Unplug the tablet, open the doors with the paper forms, and come back to the tablet once the morning rush is over.
examples.whyItMatters: The forty minutes are gone either way, and five more spent on the tablet could leave sick patients waiting in the rain.

questions.prompt: Your neighbor bought a pricey theater season ticket, then moved two hours away. He drives to every show, exhausted on the way home, saying the ticket cost too much to waste. What is the trap?
choices: Driving alone each time instead of finding someone to share the long trip.
Buying a season ticket before he knew where he would live.
Letting the ticket's old price decide how he spends each evening now.
questions.explanation: The ticket's price is spent whether he goes or not, so each trip should be judged on what it costs tonight. Sharing the drive only makes a trip he's taking for the wrong reason a little easier.

questions.prompt: A pet groomer has paid monthly fees for two years on a booking app that brings in very few customers. She asks whether she would sign up for it today, decides no, and cancels. What most likely happens next?
choices: Her few app customers stop coming, and her shop's total sales start to slip.
The two years of fees become a loss she can't recover.
The monthly fees stop, and that money goes where her customers already are.
questions.explanation: The two years of fees were gone whether she kept the app or not, so canceling adds no new loss. It just stops the monthly drain and frees that money for what is working.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I've spent eight months on my recipe blog. Hardly anyone reads it and I dread every post, but I can't stop after all that work." What is your best reply?
choices: "Write down why the blog first mattered to you, and let that keep you going."
"If you hadn't started it, would you begin it today, knowing what it takes?"
"Post once a week instead, so it takes fewer evenings while it grows."
questions.explanation: Asking if your friend would start it today leaves the eight months out and weighs only the evenings ahead. Posting less still keeps the blog alive for the old reason, the months already spent.

questions.prompt: A man spent a year restoring an old sailboat that still leaks. He asks himself what he would pay for the boat as it sits today. The answer is far less than the repairs it still needs, so he sells it. Why did his question help?
choices: It left the year he had already spent out of the decision.
It made him admit how badly he had misjudged the boat at the start.
It showed the boat was now worth less than he paid.
questions.explanation: Asking what he'd pay today leaves out the year of work, which is gone whether he keeps the boat or not. Comparing today's value with what he paid would drag that old spending right back in.

questions.prompt: You spent three weeks building a custom task tracker for your team. It keeps breaking, and the team prefers the simple shared list. Tonight you sit down to spend another evening on it. What do you do?
choices: Finish this one fix first, then decide once it works.
Ask the team which new features would finally get them to use it.
Ask whether you'd start it today, given the evenings it still needs.
questions.explanation: The three weeks are gone either way. What matters is whether the evenings it still needs beat the simple list. Fixing it first means paying for those evenings before you have even asked.

questions.prompt: A company has spent a year on a new fitness watch that test buyers keep rejecting. The boss says, "We've come too far to stop," and asks for six more months. Where does the boss's thinking go wrong?
choices: Not testing with buyers until a full year had passed.
Treating the year already spent as a reason for six more months.
Trusting a small group of test buyers over the whole team's own judgment.
questions.explanation: The year is spent whether they stop or not, so it can't be a reason to keep going. Testing sooner might have saved money, but it doesn't change what the next six months will cost.

questions.prompt: A man has paid for a storage unit for three years, full of boxes he never opens. He keeps paying because otherwise all those fees would be wasted. What will probably happen over the next year?
choices: He pays a fourth year of fees for boxes he still won't open.
The things in the boxes gain enough value to cover all the fees so far.
He finally clears it out and sells what is inside.
questions.explanation: He is treating three years of fees as the reason to pay more, so the same pull is still at work. Nothing in his thinking has changed, so the boxes stay shut and the fees keep coming.

reviewCards.front: Why doesn't quitting a failing plan waste the money you already put into it?
reviewCards.back: Because that money is gone whether you stay or quit. Only what you would spend from now on can still be saved.

reviewCards.front: When you catch yourself thinking 'I've put too much in to stop now,' the question to ask is ...
reviewCards.back: ... whether you would sign up today for what it will cost from here, with the past spending left out.

reviewCards.front: A woman kept her struggling yoga studio open another year so the first two years wouldn't be wasted, and lost most of her savings. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: She let money that was already gone choose her next year. Judged only on what that year would cost, closing was the cheaper choice.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what do you do when something you've put a lot into is failing?
reviewCards.back: Set aside what's already in it and ask only whether it's worth what it will cost from here.

reviewCards.front: You're halfway through a paid evening Italian course you've come to dread, with six classes left.
reviewCards.back: Ask whether you'd pay today for those six classes. If not, stop going and take the evenings back.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Deciding whether to keep a struggling commitment by its future costs alone, leaving past spending out.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down to put more time into a project that's stalling, I ask whether I'd start it today for what it still needs, and stop if not.
When I catch myself thinking I've put too much in to quit, I write down what staying will cost from here and decide on that alone.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, pick one subscription, class or plan you keep paying for because of what you've already put in. Ask if you'd sign up today, and cancel it if not.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, when you sit down to plan the days ahead, pick one ongoing commitment. Ask whether you'd join it today for what it will cost from here, and drop it if not.

chapters.title: Cut the Extras So What Matters Stands Out
chapters.hook: A new morning journal looks like the push a crowded week needs. Add it, and the deadline that truly matters slips further down the list.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think a better week comes from adding good things, like a new routine or a side project. Actually, it comes from cutting what doesn't belong, because every extra thing eats the hours the few important ones need and hides them in the crowd.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Act as the editor of your own week: cut what doesn't belong so what matters stands out.
chapters.tryThisNow: Open this week's to-do list now and cross out one item that does nothing for the thing that matters most to you.

memorableLines.text: Your week, like a good film, gets better in the cutting room.

breakdown.fastRead:
It is Sunday night, and Dario's nursing course application is due in three weeks. His personal statement is one paragraph long, and if it's late, he waits a year. His week already holds three gym sessions, a chess club on Thursdays and a Saturday bike ride. Now he plans to start a morning journal too.

Every extra thing, however good, eats the same hours, and the statement gets lost in the crowd. Greg McKeown says to handle your life the way an editor handles a film. A good editor makes a film stronger mostly by cutting scenes, and nobody watching sees the cuts. With the small stuff gone, the important part is easier to see and stronger. Jack Dorsey, while he ran the company Square, saw himself as its chief editor. Square could chase many things, and his job was to pick the one or two that mattered.

So Dario reads his week like an editor, asking whether each item helps the statement. The journal waits, and chess stops until the deadline. Then he condenses, which means shrinking what stays: two gym sessions, a shorter ride. By Thursday night, in the old chess hour, he has a full draft. Stop adding good things to a crowded week, and cut what doesn't belong so the one that matters stands out.

breakdown.fullRead:
It is Sunday night, and Dario's nursing course application is due in three weeks. His personal statement is one paragraph long, and if it's late, he waits a year for the next intake. His week already holds three gym sessions, a chess club on Thursdays and a long Saturday bike ride. Tonight he read about the power of a morning journal. He plans to start one on Monday, and it feels like the push his week needs.

That is the move most people would make. When life feels stuck, you add something: a new habit, a new project, a fresh idea. Each one looks good on its own. Nothing seems to be given up, because the cost is never written next to it. So the list grows, and it feels like growing as a person.

It is the move that will sink him. Every extra thing, however good, eats the same hours and the same attention. The statement is not losing to anything bad. It is losing to a crowd of nice things, each asking for a little. Greg McKeown warns that almost everything is noise, meaning it fills time without mattering much. Only a few things truly count, and someone who keeps adding never finds them. If you don't pick the few yourself, a busy week picks for you.

McKeown's answer is to handle your life the way an editor handles a film or a book. A good editor makes the work stronger mostly by taking things out. A scene can be well made and still slow the story down, so it goes. Nobody watching sees the cuts. They only see a clear story, which is why the craft goes unnoticed. With the small stuff gone, the important part is easier to see. It is stronger too, because it no longer shares the stage.

Jack Dorsey, while he ran the company Square, saw his own job this way. He thought of himself as the company's chief editor. Square could chase many things, and his work was to pick the one or two that really mattered. A crowded week works the same way, only smaller.

Cutting is the first step, and McKeown adds three more. Condensing means making what stays smaller so it does more with less, like a long meeting turned into a short one. Correcting means checking along the way that you are still on course, and fixing it when you drift. The last step is editing less. A good editor knows when a scene already works and leaves it alone instead of fiddling with it.

To use this, read next week's plan the way an editor reads a draft. Ask of each line whether it helps the one thing that matters most right now. Every line you keep is a trade-off, a choice that takes time from something else. So the lines that don't help come out, and what stays gets trimmed to its useful core. Then look again midweek, because cut things have a way of creeping back.

So Dario reads his week like an editor, asking whether each item helps the statement. The journal waits, and chess stops until the deadline. Then he condenses: two gym sessions instead of three, and a shorter Saturday ride. On Wednesday he checks again and finds he has drifted into an hour of chess videos, so he closes the app. By Thursday night, in the old chess hour, he has a full draft. Nobody will see what he cut, only a strong application. Stop adding good things to a crowded week, and cut what doesn't belong so the one that matters stands out.

examples.title: A brochure buried under good ideas
examples.scenario: Saoirse writes ads and web copy for clients from a desk by her living room window. By Friday she owes a brochure to her biggest client, who covers half her rent. Monday's plan also lists a new portfolio site, a daily post online, two coffee chats and a free trial of an invoicing app. It is nine o'clock, and she hasn't written a word of the brochure.
examples.whatToDo: Strike the portfolio site, the daily posts and the app trial until Friday, keep one coffee chat, and give every morning to the brochure.
examples.whyItMatters: With the extras gone, the brochure gets her freshest hours, and the client paying half her rent gets her best work.

examples.title: When more revision made the grade worse
examples.scenario: Kenji's chemistry exam is in two weeks, and his last mock was a C. So he added things: a lunchtime study group, a flashcard app with a daily streak, and an hour of revision before school. He kept robotics club and his gaming nights too. Yesterday's practice test came back lower than the mock, and he nodded off in history.
examples.whatToDo: Drop the early hour and the streak, pause robotics and gaming until the exam, and keep the study group for his weakest topics.
examples.whyItMatters: Each new tool ate the same tired hours. With less going on, chemistry finally gets his full attention.

examples.title: Getting the house ready for a visit
examples.scenario: Beatriz's parents arrive Saturday, their first visit since her father's heart surgery. Her list says repaint the hallway, wash every curtain, bake three cakes and clear the shed. Her sister offered to bring dessert, but Beatriz always bakes, and saying yes felt like admitting she couldn't cope. At eleven on Thursday night she is scrubbing the oven, proud of the list and too tired to enjoy any of it.
examples.whatToDo: Cross off the paint and the shed, text her sister yes to dessert, and keep Saturday afternoon free for a slow walk with her dad.
examples.whyItMatters: Her parents won't notice the curtains. They will remember an easy afternoon with a daughter who had time for them.

questions.prompt: A woman who runs a bike repair shop wants this spring to be about her new repair classes. She drops a loyalty card scheme and a window redesign for now and gives the classes her time. What most likely happens?
choices: The classes get her best hours and start strong, and nobody misses the dropped plans.
The shop looks dull without fresh ideas, and regular customers slowly drift away.
The classes still struggle, since a single plan alone can't carry a small shop through spring.
questions.explanation: With the extras dropped, the classes get her time and attention, and like an editor's cuts, the missing plans go unnoticed. Fresh ideas won't keep customers if the main one launches half-done.

questions.prompt: A friend says her evenings vanish into scrolling and group chats. She plans to add a language class and a nightly run to make them count. What do you tell her?
choices: "Good plan. Start the class this week and add the run once it settles."
"Keep everything, but give each thing a little less time so the class and the run fit."
"First see what your evenings already hold, and clear out the bits you don't care about."
questions.explanation: Her evenings are already full, so adding two things only deepens the crowd. Clearing out what she doesn't care about gives whatever matters room. Giving everything a little less time keeps all the clutter.

questions.prompt: A gardener studying for a tree-care exam drops his Sunday lawn-mowing side job and a new running plan until the exam. Within two weeks his practice scores climb. Why did the cuts help?
choices: Less stress made him calmer, and a calmer person simply remembers more facts.
Giving things up proved to himself he was serious, and that belief kept him studying hard.
The exam stopped sharing his hours with other things, so it got his full attention.
questions.explanation: The exam no longer shared his hours with the mowing and the runs, so it got his full attention. Feeling serious adds no study time. The cuts worked by freeing it.

questions.prompt: You restore old chairs in a rented workshop, and a café's order for twelve chairs is due this month. Monday's list also holds a newsletter, a new video channel, re-sorting your tools and two craft fair forms. What do you do first?
choices: Set yourself a hard Friday deadline for the order, and tell the café about it.
Go through Monday's list and drop whatever does nothing for the café's chair order.
Get the quick jobs done first, then give the chairs the time left.
questions.explanation: Dropping what doesn't serve the order clears room, so the chairs get your hours. Doing quick jobs first sounds tidy, but they eat the same day and leave the order the scraps.

questions.prompt: A dad wants more evenings at home with his two kids. He keeps his Tuesday squash and his Thursday overtime, and signs up for a parenting course on Wednesdays. What trap did he fall into?
choices: Booking the course on a weeknight, when a weekend class would fit better.
Adding a good thing to his week instead of clearing what keeps him away.
Leaving each evening plan at full length, instead of trimming all of them a little.
questions.explanation: The course is a good thing, but it took one of the very evenings he wanted. Clearing what keeps him away would free nights at home. Moving the course to a weekend still adds, just elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A family-run guesthouse drops its bike hire, packed lunches and guided walks, and puts that effort into its rooms and breakfasts. What will guests most likely write in reviews?
choices: They praise the rooms and breakfast, and hardly anyone mentions the missing extras.
They complain that the guesthouse feels bare without the old extras.
They barely notice a change, since the extras were never what drew them in.
questions.explanation: The effort once spread across extras now goes into rooms and breakfast, so those get better, and that's what guests notice. The cuts go unseen. Saying nothing changed misses how the main things grew stronger.

questions.prompt: A coworker cleared her week a month ago to finish a big project. She tells you it worked for two weeks, but now her calendar is full again and clearing it just doesn't stick. What is the most useful answer?
choices: "Maybe the project was the wrong focus, so pick a new one."
"Look over your week again every so often, and clear out what crept back."
"Cut everything except the project for now, so nothing else has room to creep back."
questions.explanation: An editor keeps checking that the work stays on course, so one clear-out isn't the end. Looking again removes what crept back. Cutting all but the project would also drop things that do belong.
